source.title: Hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods for second-order elliptic problems: overview, a new result and open problems

accepted.question_text: For hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods for second-order elliptic problems, fix the local spaces used by the lowest-index hybridized Raviart-Thomas method and determine which new stabilization functions, together with any corresponding spaces they induce, make the resulting lowest-degree HDG method superconvergent, despite the fact that the usual lowest-degree HDG method is not superconvergent. The same question should also be examined for the related schemes of Huerta et al.

evidence.quote: Superconvergence of lowest degree HDG methods. The hybridized Raviart-Thomas method of lowest index k=0 superconverges, but the usual HDG method does not; see [ 12 ]. However, we just saw that it can be rewritten as an HDG method using the spaces ... with a very particular stabilization. If we fix the local spaces, one wonders what is the class of new stabilizations (and the corresponding spaces!) which also render the corresponding HDG method superconvergent. The approach could also be applied to the schemes proposed by Huerta et al. in [ 98 ].

accepted.question_text: Construct new M-decompositions beyond the cases already developed for V_g(K) × W_g(K) = P_k(K) × P_k(K), specifically by working out the case in which a = Id and V_g(K) × W_g(K) = ∇W(K) × W(K).

evidence.quote: New M-decompositions. The known M-decompositions, see [ 27 , 28 , 55 ] and [ 30 , 54 ], have been developed for V_g(K)×W_g(K):=P_k(K)×P_k(K) only. It would be interesting to work out the case set a:=Id and V_g(K)×W_g(K):=∇W(K)×W(K).

accepted.question_text: Can the construction of the spaces appearing in M-decompositions be reformulated entirely in terms of the corresponding stabilization functions, so that one can construct stabilizations directly and thereby avoid the potentially difficult explicit construction of the auxiliary space V_s(K)?

evidence.quote: Bypassing the construction of the spaces for M-decompositions. It should be possible to rewrite the construction of the spaces of M-decompositions in terms of their respective stabilizations. The construction of the stabilization functions seems to be simpler than the construction of the corresponding spaces, and so, we could bypass the latter and go directly with the former. In this way, the potentially difficult construction of the actual space V_s(K) could be bypassed.

accepted.question_text: Using the fact that mixed methods can be viewed as hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods, develop an automatic way to translate adaptive-convergence results that are known for mixed methods into corresponding adaptive-convergence results for HDG methods.
accepted.context_brief: Adaptivity transfer from mixed to HDG

evidence.quote: Adaptivity. In the 2016 paper [ 53 ], the first convergence of an adaptive method for an HDG method was proposed. On the other hand, results of that sort for mixed methods are not difficult to find in the literature. By using that mixed methods are also HDG methods, there could be an automatic way to translate the results for the mixed methods into the corresponding results for the HDG methods.

accepted.question_text: Rework the conclusions of the 2022 variational multiscale analysis of discontinuous Galerkin and mixed methods so that they correctly reflect the paper's new observation that mixed methods are also HDG methods.

evidence.quote: Variational multiscale analysis for HDG methods. In the 2022 paper [ 97 ], a variational multiscale anlysis of DG (and mixed) methods was presented. Since here we establish that mixed methods are also HDG method, one wonders how the conclusions of that paper should be altered to fit this fact.

accepted.question_text: Can the exact-sequence constructions and commuting diagrams obtained from M-decompositions and mixed-method spaces be rewritten in terms of the spaces of the corresponding HDG methods, in a way that yields exact sequences for discontinuous Galerkin methods?

evidence.quote: Exact sequences for DG methods. In the 2017 paper [ 29 ], a systematic way of constructing exact sequences, see [ 2 ], was presented which was based on the work on M-decompositions [ 27 , 28 , 55 ]. In the last part of the sequences, the spaces of a mixed method are used. Since, mixed methods can be recast as HDG methods, the corresponding commuting diagrams could be rewritten in terms of the spaces for the HDG method potentially giving rise to exact sequences for DG methods.

accepted.question_text: Extend the steady-state diffusion framework developed in the paper to time-dependent problems, including the heat equation and mixed-method formulations for wave propagation, and determine whether the resulting methods are equivalent to HDG methods whose numerical fluxes contain time derivatives.

evidence.quote: The time-dependent case. What has been presented here for steady-state diffusion could be extended to the time-dependent case, not only for the heat equation but for mixed methods for wave propagation problems. The resulting methods might be equivalent to some of the newly found HDG methods with time-derivatives in their numerical fluxes [ 58 ].

accepted.question_text: Extend the Section 5 transformation results to other discretization families: first to hybridized versions of augmented mixed methods in which an auxiliary variable g_h is introduced and the approximate flux q_h is defined from q_h = a g_h when c = a^{-1} is hard to compute; and then, if possible, to the continuous Galerkin method, potentially via the Staggered DG method or via Voralík's orthogonal-projection result for locally postprocessed mixed methods.

evidence.quote: Other methods. When the matrix c:=a^{-1} is not easy to compute, one can define the auxiliary variable g_h∈V_h ... to define the approximate flux q_h∈V_h ... Extending the results of Sect. 5 to the hybridized form of these sometimes called augmented mixed methods should be immediate; see the analysis in the 2018 paper [ 57 ].

The extension of these results to the continuous Galerkin method is an interesting possibility. Maybe the extension to the Staggered DG method [ 13 ] would provide a way to proceed in that case, because this method displays partial continuity of the scalar unkown and because it has been proved to be a limiting case of HDG methods; see [ 14 , 15 ]. Another possibility is to use a result by Voralík [ 100 , Theorem 7.1] which establishes that the solution of the continuous Galerkin method is an orthogonal projection of the locally postprocessed mixed method.

accepted.question_text: Push the space-versus-stabilization ideas of the paper beyond steady-state diffusion to other partial differential equations, including steady-state elasticity, the Stokes equations of incompressible flow, and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, and especially investigate whether those ideas can produce new numerical schemes for nonlinear hyperbolic problems in which new approximation spaces, rather than only new stabilizations, lead to improved DG methods.
accepted.context_brief: Other PDEs and nonlinear hyperbolic DG

evidence.quote: Other PDEs. Expanding these results to other partial differential equations constitutes a challenging and interesting udertaking worth of further exploration. An incipient effort in this direction has been made in recent years. Indeed, M-decompositions have been developed in [ 18 , 30 ], for steady-state elasticity; in [ 54 ], for the Stokes equations of incompressible flow; and in [ 56 ], for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations.

The development of DG methods would give a full circle if it would be possible to use the ideas of the relation of a space and a stabilization uncovered in Theorem 5.1 to devise new numerical schemes for nonlinear hyperbolic problems. So far, the use of suitable stabilizations have been extremely successful in this area, but the use of new spaces could potentially bring new and, why not?, better schemes. The general formulation for the numerical traces, obtained in the 2015 paper by Bui-Thanh [ 10 ], should be a useful result in this endeavor.

accepted.question_text: Develop a systematic procedure that transforms stabilizations into spaces, reversing the direction of Theorem 5.1, so that any HDG method can be rewritten as a mixed method in a mathematically useful way that exposes genuinely new approximation spaces and may even produce a discontinuous Galerkin method for pure convection with no stabilization function.

evidence.quote: Transforming stabilizations into spaces. Let us elaborate this last idea a little further. Theorem 5.1 shows how to transform spaces into stabilizations, but it seems possible to transform stabilizations into spaces too. As a consequence, we could then rewrite any HDG method as a mixed method. Of course, we do not want just to change the way of presenting the original HDG scheme. So, we could look for the possibility of using new spaces which would render the scheme better. In particular, this would mean that we could have a DG method for pure convection problems without stabilization function.

accepted.question_text: Find routes to superconvergence for general hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods that do not satisfy the usual boundary-trace inclusion properties required by the M-decomposition framework. In particular, explain whether the two currently known classes—methods that compensate by specially defined projections of numerical traces, and methods related to hybrid high-order methods with sophisticated stabilizations—can be related back to hybridized mixed methods through a reversed version of Theorem 5.1.

evidence.quote: Are there other ways of achieving superconvergence? We have relied on the theory of M-decompositions to obtain superconvergent HM and HDG methods defined in elements of general shape. To be able to use the M-decompositions, we have assumed that the local spaces satisfy the inclusion properties ... The general HDG methods, however, do not to satisfy these properties.

Currently, there are two known classes of HDG methods which do not satisfy them. One of them, roughly speaking, compensates the lack of these inclusions by using a suitable defined projection of the numerical traces. Optimal convergence, and superconvergence of the numerical traces are thus obtained for elements of general shape.

A second class of those methods are HDG methods related to the hybrid high-order (HHO) methods introduced in 2014 in [ 62 ] and in 2015 in [ 61 ] (for linear elasticity); see also the books [ 16 , 60 ]. As shown in 2015 in [ 52 ], they can be rewritten as HDG method with a new, sophisticated stabilization function devised to achieve optimal convergence and superconvergence of some of the numerical traces for elements of general shape. These two classes of methods already achieve the wanted convergence properties, but one wonders if there is a way to relate them with HM methods in what one could call a reversed version of Theorem 5.1 . The work done in 2020 by Du and Sayas [ 64 ] can be considered to be a first step towards that goal.

accepted.question_text: For spectral postprocessing of HDG methods, determine—by importing the techniques behind Theorem 5.1 and comparing with the mixed-method construction in [49]—what was missing either from the earlier HDG approach or from the HDG methods it studied, so that one could achieve convergence order 2k+2 instead of only 2k+1.

evidence.quote: Spectral postprocessing. In [ 67 ], a similar approach for HDG methods could only provide an order of convergence of 2k+1. One wonders if by applying the techniques leading to Theorem 5.1 to what was done in [ 49 ] for mixed methods, one could identify what was missing in the approach used, or in the HDG methods considered, in [ 67 ] to obtain order 2k+2.

accepted.question_text: Work out negative-order norm error estimates and postprocessing results for mixed methods, using the known hierarchy in which the H^{-(k+1)}(Ω)-error order is 2k for continuous Galerkin, 2k+1 for discontinuous Galerkin, and 2k+2 for mixed methods, and then use Theorem 5.1 to identify which stabilizations allow HDG methods to achieve H^{-(k+1)}(Ω)-error order 2k+2 as well.

evidence.quote: Negative-order norm estimates. A related issue is the problem of error estimation in negative-order norms.

The above procedures should be able to be extented to mixed methods with a better order of convergence. Indeed, the H^{-(k+1)}(Ω)-norm of the error is 2k for the continuous Galerkin method, 2k+1 for the DG method, and 2k+2 for the mixed method. So, it would be interesting to work out these result for mixed methods and then apply Theorem 5.1 in order to see what type of stabilizations allow HDG methods to have the H^{-(k+1)}(Ω)-norm of the errors of order 2k+2.
